{"artifact":"SmeDossierEnvelope","schema_version":"0.4.0","stage_id":"02.dossier_sections","probe":"rdmv-mo-f","lineage":{"input_manifest_sha256":"7b6a511e17bf2970caca15ad4343379264f62f6a1f39653f5db0f0d08eea5934","candidate_lineage_id":"2026-10-28-rdmv-mo-class-f:lineage:51","source_registry_sha256":"f128002157e581eb7004b9370c8cfbafd7b29a1596262980704fbda0a45932f5","source_liveness_sha256":"fdf72d02e75b9589fee5aaf5b83ec9705ff03586f574464e3553a827f9b698d8"},"envelope_scope":{"kind":"partial_chunk","assigned_section_ids":["C2"],"chunk_index":1,"chunk_total":1},"section_char_limit":12000,"sections":[{"section_id":"C2","chunk_id":"C2.01","merge_seq":1,"domain":"Alcohol and drugs look-alikes: BAC limits by driver, Abuse and Lose versus Minor in Possession, the two fees, refusal versus interlock penalties, and continuation facts on effects and help","heading":"C2 — Confusable pairs and continuation facts: the three BAC limits, the two fifteen-day periods, Abuse and Lose versus Minor in Possession, the two reinstatement fees, interlock extras, medicine cautions, marijuana with alcohol, and substance use help","learner_facing":false,"markdown":"## C2 — Confusable pairs and continuation facts: the three BAC limits, the two fifteen-day periods, Abuse and Lose versus Minor in Possession, the two reinstatement fees, interlock extras, medicine cautions, marijuana with alcohol, and substance use help
Confusable pairs among the alcohol and drug rules, plus continuation facts that complete part C; each block ties to one guide page, the penalty charts are tables whose layout was partly lost in text extraction so only cells with a clear row and column are used, and hint metadata sits only in the trailing line of a block.

FACT_ID: sec12-R01 | anchor: A05
The legal BAC limit depends on the driver: 0.08% for most drivers, 0.04% for commercial vehicle drivers, and 0.02% for drivers under 21. [A05]
Why it matters: group BAC limits; confusable limits by driver type; difficulty high.
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0073]

FACT_ID: sec12-R02 | anchor: A01
Two different fifteen-day periods appear on the arrest notice page: the license is lost 15 days after the notice, and with a hearing you may drive until 15 days after the decision is mailed. [A01]
Why it matters: group administrative action; confusable notice period versus hearing period; difficulty high.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0069]

FACT_ID: sec12-R03 | anchor: A03
Abuse and Lose takes the license for 90 days from a driver under 21, but for a full year from a driver 21 or older who has or uses drugs while driving. [A03]
Why it matters: group youth rules; confusable under versus over twenty-one; difficulty high.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0071]

FACT_ID: sec12-R04 | anchor: A03
A first Minor in Possession offense brings a 30-day suspension, which is shorter than the 90-day loss under Abuse and Lose. [A03]
Why it matters: group youth rules; confusable Minor in Possession versus Abuse and Lose; difficulty medium.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0071]

FACT_ID: sec12-R05 | anchor: A04
The $45 fee is the reinstatement fee after an intoxication-related offense, while a separate $20 fee applies when reinstating after the interlock was not maintained. [A04]
Why it matters: group fees; confusable reinstatement fee versus interlock fee; difficulty medium.
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0072]

FACT_ID: sec12-R06 | anchor: A04
Refusing a chemical test and being convicted of not installing a required interlock both cost one year of driving privilege. [A04]
Why it matters: group refusal and interlock; confusable equal one-year penalties; difficulty medium.
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0072]

FACT_ID: sec12-R07 | anchor: A04
Six months is the least time an interlock must stay installed after reinstatement, but a court may order a device for longer than six months. [A04]
Why it matters: group interlock; confusable minimum versus court-ordered period; difficulty medium.
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0072]

FACT_ID: sec12-R08 | anchor: A02
Only a BAC conviction dated August 28, 2009 or later can be counted toward a five-year license denial. [A02]
Why it matters: group court action; difficulty high.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0070]

FACT_ID: sec12-R09 | anchor: A01
Being found guilty of drinking or using drugs while driving in Missouri can bring a fine, a lost license, and even jail. [A01]
Why it matters: group penalties; continuation of the chapter opening.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0069]

FACT_ID: sec12-R10 | anchor: A04
A court may also require an interlock after a first DWI conviction, beyond what the licensing rules require. [A04]
Why it matters: group interlock; continuation of court requirements.
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0072]

FACT_ID: sec12-R11 | anchor: A04
If you fail to keep the interlock, your driving privilege is suspended again until the device is serviced or installed and proof is sent to the Driver License Bureau. [A04]
Why it matters: group interlock; continuation of re-suspension.
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0072]

FACT_ID: sec12-R12 | anchor: A05
Alcohol can also cause drowsiness, weaker concentration and attention, poorer coordination and comprehension, and worse decisions. [A05]
Why it matters: group alcohol effects; continuation of effects.
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0073]

FACT_ID: sec12-R13 | anchor: A05
It is illegal for anyone under 21 to possess or buy alcohol in Missouri. [A05]
Why it matters: group youth rules; difficulty low.
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0073]

FACT_ID: sec12-R14 | anchor: A05
The effects page restates the DWI punishment as up to six months in prison, a fine of up to $500, and loss of driving privileges. [A05]
Why it matters: group penalties; restates the first conviction row.
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0073]

FACT_ID: sec12-R15 | anchor: A05
Cold and allergy medicines bought over the counter can make you drowsy and hurt your driving. [A05]
Why it matters: group medicines; difficulty low.
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0073]

FACT_ID: sec12-R16 | anchor: A05
Pep pills, uppers and diet pills may make a driver more alert for a short time but later can cause nervousness, dizziness, poor concentration and vision problems. [A05]
Why it matters: group medicines; confusable short-term alert versus later impairment; difficulty medium.
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0073]

FACT_ID: sec12-R17 | anchor: A05
Do not take any drug whose label warns that it may cause drowsiness or dizziness before you drive. [A05]
Why it matters: group medicines; difficulty low.
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0073]

FACT_ID: sec12-R18 | anchor: A05
Taking a medicine prescribed for someone else is both dangerous and illegal, and you should not mix medicines unless your doctor tells you to. [A05]
Why it matters: group medicines; difficulty low.
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0073]

FACT_ID: sec12-R19 | anchor: A05
Never combine alcohol with any medicine, because many drugs have unexpected side effects when taken with alcohol. [A05]
Why it matters: group medicines; difficulty low.
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0073]

FACT_ID: sec12-R20 | anchor: A06
Drivers who used alcohol together with marijuana were even more impaired, with still more lane weaving, than with marijuana alone. [A06]
Why it matters: group marijuana; confusable combined versus single substance; difficulty medium.
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0074]

FACT_ID: sec12-R21 | anchor: A06
A substance use disorder is repeated alcohol or drug use that causes serious problems such as health issues, disability, or failing duties at work, school or home. [A06]
Why it matters: group substance use; glossary substance use disorder.
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0074]

FACT_ID: sec12-R22 | anchor: A06
People with a substance use disorder are at greater risk of hurting themselves or others in a motor vehicle crash. [A06]
Why it matters: group substance use; difficulty low.
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0074]

FACT_ID: sec12-R23 | anchor: A06
Help for a substance use disorder is available through the free, confidential SAMHSA National Helpline, open around the clock every day of the year. [A06]
Why it matters: group substance use; difficulty low.
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0074]

FACT_ID: sec12-R24 | anchor: A06
Early use is one of the strongest predictors of addiction, because a young brain that is still developing can be damaged faster and more severely than an adult brain. [A06]
Why it matters: group substance use; difficulty medium.
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0074]
